lessons.title: Maps, coordinate distances and translations
lessons.summary: Use a scale, measure along one coordinate direction and identify translated points without a grid.
lessons.objective: Use a scale, measure along one coordinate direction and identify translated points without a grid.
lessons.before: A map scale tells you what one unit on the drawing represents in real life.
lessons.ideas:
Multiply by the amount represented by one map unit to find a real distance. Divide the real distance by that amount to find a map distance.

Subtract the smaller changing coordinate from the larger one. The result is a distance, so it cannot be negative.

Right increases x and up increases y. Left decreases x and down decreases y.
lessons.method:
Label the map and real measurements in your working.

Start by naming the coordinate that changes.

Write the two signed moves before applying them to a point.
mistakes: Check the units on both sides of the scale. Map centimetres and real kilometres are different units.
Include the distance on both sides of zero when a segment crosses zero.
The vertical move changes only the second coordinate.

examples.title: A map of a cycle route
examples.question:
The map uses a scale of 1 cm for every 1 km. The route between a farm and a station is 5 cm long on the map.

  1. Find the real length of the route.

    [2]

  2. An extra ride is 5 km. How long is that extra ride on the map?

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) Each one-centimetre part represents 1 km.

Multiply 5 by 1.

\(5\) km.

(b) Divide 5 km by 1 km per map centimetre.

\(5\) cm.

examples.title: Finding a distance without a grid
examples.question:
Points A and B have coordinates \((1,-17)\) and \((1,2)\).

  1. Find the distance from A to B.

    [2]

  2. Explain whether the segment AB is horizontal or vertical.

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) The y-coordinate changes from -17 to 2.

Subtract -17 from 2 to find the positive distance.

\(19\) units.

(b) One coordinate stays the same along the whole segment.

Vertical, because the x-values agree.

examples.title: A move on the coordinate plane
examples.question:
One vertex of a shape is \((-13,-12)\). The whole shape moves right 8 units and down 6 units.

  1. Give the coordinates of the new vertex.

    [2]

  2. Explain what has happened to the side lengths of the shape.

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) Add 8 to the x-coordinate.

Subtract 6 from the y-coordinate.

\((-5,-18)\).

(b) Every point moves by the same amount and in the same direction.

The side lengths stay the same.

lessons.title: Reflection, rotation and enlargement
lessons.summary: Reflect points across an axis, make quarter and half turns, and enlarge shapes from a centre.
lessons.objective: Reflect points across an axis, make quarter and half turns, and enlarge shapes from a centre.
lessons.before: Each point and its image have the same perpendicular distance from the mirror line. For a mirror axis, the coordinate along it stays fixed.
lessons.ideas:
In the x-axis, keep x and reverse y. In the y-axis, keep y and reverse x.

A 90° turn is a quarter turn and a 180° turn is a half turn. A rotation keeps distances and angles unchanged.

For scale factor 2, place the image vertex twice as far along the ray. Equal angles and the same scale factor give similar shapes.
lessons.method:
Use the line named in the question as your mirror.

Use tracing paper or count grid steps from the centre to check.

Describe an enlargement using both its centre and scale factor.
mistakes: Do not change both signs for one reflection in a coordinate axis.
Check the direction. Clockwise and anticlockwise quarter turns give different positions.
An enlargement is measured from its centre. Do not simply double coordinates if the centre is somewhere else.

examples.title: Reflecting a point across an axis
examples.question:
A vertex has coordinates \((5,2)\). Reflect its shape in the x-axis.

  1. Give the new coordinates of this vertex.

    [2]

  2. For two more vertices \((7,2)\) and \((5,5)\), find their images.

    [2]

  3. Would the original shape and its image be congruent?

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) Keep the coordinate measured along the x-axis.

Reverse the sign of the other coordinate.

\((5,-2)\).

(b) Reflect each vertex in the same axis.

The coordinates are \((7,-2)\) and \((5,-5)\).

(c) Each point moves to its mirror position without any stretching.

Yes. Corresponding sides and angles stay the same.

examples.title: Turning a shape around a centre
examples.question:
A triangle has vertices A \((17,0)\), B \((18,0)\) and C \((17,1)\). Rotate the shape 90° anticlockwise around \((-1,-2)\).

  1. Give the image coordinates of A.

    [2]

  2. Give the coordinates of B and C after the turn. Explain what happens to the side lengths.

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) The offset of A from the centre is \((18,2)\).

Turn that offset to \((-2,18)\), then add it to the centre's coordinates.

\((-3,16)\).

(b) Turn each offset through the same angle around the same centre.

B maps to \((-3,17)\) and C maps to \((-4,16)\). All side lengths stay the same.

examples.title: Enlarging a pattern from the origin
examples.question:
A design has a corner at \((31,1)\). Enlarge it about the origin with scale factor 3.

  1. Give the coordinates of the enlarged corner.

    [2]

  2. Give the image positions of two more vertices \((32,1)\) and \((31,2)\). Describe how the side lengths change.

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) Measure the original horizontal and vertical distances from the origin.

Multiply both distances by 3.

\((93,3)\).

(b) The same factor acts on every direction.

The images are \((96,3)\) and \((93,6)\). Side lengths are multiplied by 3. Corresponding angles stay equal, so the shapes are similar.
